keyVerseText: But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites : and he killed him, and reigned in his room.
rootMeaning: The name רְמַלְיָהוּ (Remalyâhûw) derives from a root that is unused but is combined with the divine element יָהּ (Yâhh), a shortened form of Jehovah, signifying the Lord. The etymology suggests a meaning along the lines of 'Jah has bedecked' or 'protected by Jehovah,' indicating a divine adornment or safeguarding. This literal sense enriches the common English gloss 'protected by Jehovah' by emphasizing not only protection but also a sense of being honored or set apart by God.
usageInScripture: The word רְמַלְיָהוּ appears thirteen times in Scripture, predominantly as a proper name referring to the father of King Pekah of Israel. Its translations are consistent, with 'of Remaliah' appearing eleven times, and occasional variations such as 'is Remaliah's' or 'and Remaliah's,' all indicating possession or association. This consistency reflects the name's role as a marker of lineage and identity within the historical narrative of Israel's northern kingdom.
theologicalSignificance: The name Remaliah, meaning 'protected by Jehovah,' highlights the biblical theme of God's sovereign protection over His people and their leaders, even amid political turmoil. Recognizing the divine element within the name reminds believers that earthly rulers and events unfold under God's providential care. For the Christian faith, this underscores the truth that God is ultimately in control, guarding His purposes and those He appoints, pointing forward to the perfect protection found in Christ. It invites reflection on how God adorns and preserves His covenant community throughout history.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 15:25, the phrase 'Pekah the son of Remaliah' identifies Pekah's lineage, grounding his identity and authority in his father Remaliah. This connection emphasizes that Pekah's actions and reign are part of a divine narrative involving God's protection and judgment. The name Remaliah here reminds readers that even in the midst of rebellion and political intrigue, God's sovereign protection and purposes are at work, shaping Israel's history according to His will.
